vignette:
At twenty-four, he works as a financial analyst in a downtown office where the days are measured in spreadsheets, earnings calls, and small corrections that matter a great deal. He is good at the work because he notices patterns quickly and rarely misses an inconsistency. His coworkers see him as disciplined, quiet, and unusually composed for someone his age. They do not see how much effort it takes for him to sit with his back to the open room, or how often he glances toward the glass door when someone enters too fast.

He grew up in a close Latin American family where duty is spoken about plainly and sacrifice is expected rather than praised. He enlisted young, wanting structure, pride, and a way to help his family. When he talks about deployment, he does so carefully, as if he is stepping across unstable ground. At first he tells the story in broad pieces: heat, dust, long stretches of waiting, joking with other men to keep fear from becoming visible. Then he gets to the day that divides his life into before and after.

His convoy is moving through an area that had felt tense all morning. He remembers noticing small things he can no longer explain fully-an empty roadside, a parked vehicle that seemed wrong, the way his body had already begun to tighten before anything happened. Then there is an explosion, so loud and close that for a moment he cannot make sense of what is sound and what is pressure. The vehicle jerks, metal screams, and the air fills with smoke and dirt. He is thrown into action before he has time to think. He sees one of the men he knows well gravely injured. He remembers trying to help, shouting, hands slick, heart pounding so hard it feels like it might burst through his chest. He also remembers a terrible, lasting thought: that he should have seen it coming.

Afterward, he keeps functioning. He does what is required, finishes the deployment, and tells himself that getting through each day is the same as being okay. But his body does not seem to understand that the danger has passed. Sleep changes first. He starts waking drenched in sweat, disoriented and ready to fight. Sometimes in the dream he is back in the vehicle; sometimes he only hears the blast and wakes before he can see what comes next. Loud noises make him drop into a crouch or whip around before he can stop himself. Fireworks, slamming doors, a truck backfiring on the street-his whole body reacts as if the threat is immediate.

When he returns home, his family is relieved and proud. They cook for him, ask him to come to gatherings, tell stories about people he has not seen in years. He tries to be there, tries to smile, but the ordinary noise of family life feels unbearable. Children running behind him make him tense. If someone touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he jerks away sharply and then feels ashamed. His mother notices that he sits facing entrances in restaurants. His younger cousin laughs once about how serious he has become, and he forces a grin he does not feel.

The guilt grows quietly. He thinks about the man who did not come home and about all the tiny decisions that led to that day. He replays the route, the timing, the angle of his attention, searching for the moment he failed. He knows other people tell him it was not his fault, but the thought does not stay. It returns at night, in the shower, in traffic, in the middle of reviewing quarterly reports. He has become skilled at looking calm while his mind runs somewhere else entirely.

At work, the symptoms settle into his routine. He arrives early because crowded elevators make him uneasy and because scanning the office before others come in helps him settle. He prefers numbers to conversation; numbers stay where they are put. Still, concentration slips at odd moments. A sudden image of smoke or blood cuts through a meeting, and for several seconds he cannot hear what is being said. He keeps meticulous notes to cover these lapses. He avoids office happy hours because bars are noisy and unpredictable, and because he does not trust what might happen if he relaxes too much. He says he is busy, that he has an early morning, that he is saving money.

He has not dated seriously since coming back. When someone gets close, he begins to feel trapped by their questions or irritated by their needs. He tells himself he is protecting them from his moods, though part of him also fears being known. Some nights he walks his apartment checking the windows and lock more than once. He sleeps lightly, often on the couch with the television on low, as if a familiar voice might keep the darker images away.

By the time he speaks openly about it, he is exhausted. He says he is tired of living as though the blast is always about to happen again. Even in the safety of an office, even in his own home, part of him remains on that road, alert, braced, and unable to stand down.
